etymology: From out and the Anglo-Saxon suffix -weard, denoting direction. Webster 1828: external; exterior; visible; opposed to inward. Scripture uses the word to draw the line God draws, between what man can see and what He sees.
biblical_def: The verse that governs this word is the LORD’s correction of Samuel at the anointing of David: Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature... for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). Samuel was a prophet, and he had just been wrong about Eliab; the capacity to judge by appearance is not cured by office. Our Lord applies the same standard to the most religious men of His day: ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness (Matthew 23:27). The outward is not merely less important; where it is cultivated as a substitute it becomes a lie. Paul turns the word toward the believer’s body and finds comfort where the world finds only decline: though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). And Peter directs Christian women away from the visible to the durable: Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel (1 Peter 3:3), the next verse naming the hidden man of the heart, of great price in the sight of God.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OUTWARD as external; exterior; forming the superficial part; visible; apparent; and, in reference to the mind, foreign, adventitious, opposed to inward or spiritual.
webster_full: OUTWARD, a. — External; exterior; forming the superficial part; as the outward form.
Visible; apparent; as outward show or profession.
Adventitious; not intrinsic; as outward circumstances.
OUTWARD, adv. — To foreign parts; as a ship outward bound.
From out and -ward, Anglo-Saxon weard, direction; the opposite of inward.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 16:7

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Matthew 23:27
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness.
2 Corinthians 4:16
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
1 Peter 3:3
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
corruption_summary: 1 Samuel 16:7 is regularly quoted to mean that appearance does not matter at all; what it says is that God sees what man cannot, which makes the heart more accountable rather than the outward irrelevant.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is not a licence for indifference to the visible. Scripture cares a great deal about outward conduct: it legislates it, it makes it the test of profession, and James says faith without works is dead. What 1 Samuel 16:7 denies is that the visible is sufficient evidence, and it denies this in a context where a prophet had just misjudged. The popular use of the verse — as a warrant against any assessment of a man’s life — produces the opposite of its intent, since the reason the outward cannot be trusted is that God is examining something deeper and will not be deceived. Our Lord’s woes on the Pharisees make the same point from the other side: their outward was beautiful, and that was precisely the indictment. Hypocrisy is only possible where the outward can be managed.

1 Peter 3:3-4 has been read in two wrong directions. The first is legalistic: a prohibition of braided hair, gold, and good clothing as such — which cannot be sustained, since the same grammatical construction would forbid the putting on of apparel altogether. Peter is setting a comparison, as Scripture often does, not banning the lesser thing. The second error is the modern dismissal of the passage as cultural residue. But the positive command remains and is unaffected by culture: the adorning that God prizes is the hidden man of the heart, a meek and quiet spirit, which He calls of great price. In an age organized around the curation of an outward image, that is not a quaint verse; it is a direct contradiction of the reigning economy of attention.
roots_summary: Hebrew ayin (H5869), the eye, in the phrase to the eyes; mareh (H4758), appearance; Greek exothen (G1855), from without, outward; exo (G1854), outside.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayin (H5869) — the eye; man looketh to the eyes, rendered on the outward appearance (1 Samuel 16:7).
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart, the inner man; what the LORD looks upon instead.
Greek exothen (G1855) — from the outside, outwardly; appear beautiful outward (Matthew 23:27).
Greek exo (G1854) with anthropos — the outward man; the perishing frame of 2 Corinthians 4:16.
Greek kosmos (G2889) — ordering, adornment; the root of Peter’s adorning in 1 Peter 3:3.
usage: Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7) — spoken to a prophet who had just misjudged.
Appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones (Matthew 23:27) — hypocrisy is only possible where the outward can be managed.
Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16) — comfort where the world sees only decline.

etymology: From Latin naturalis, from natura, birth, nature, from nasci, to be born. Webster 1828: pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature; not artificial. Paul uses it for the man as he is born, and the whole doctrine of depravity hangs on the adjective.
biblical_def: Paul’s contrast between two kinds of man turns on this word, and it is one of the most consequential adjectives in Scripture: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14). Three claims are made and each is stronger than the last: he does not receive, they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them. The impediment is not information but capacity, and the remedy therefore cannot be argument alone. The same adjective distinguishes the body sown from the body raised: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not matter against spirit, but the body animated by soul against the body animated by the Spirit. James uses it of a face in a mirror: the hearer who is not a doer is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass (James 1:23), who goes his way and forgets. And Paul uses natural for the created order in sexuality: even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature (Romans 1:26).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NATURAL as pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature, or by the laws of growth; not artificial; according to the stated course of things; and of persons, unregenerate, according to the state of man by birth.
webster_full: NATURAL, a. — Pertaining to nature; produced or effected by nature, or by the laws of growth, formation or motion.
According to the stated course of things; not miraculous.
Not artificial or acquired; native; inborn; as natural affection.
Unaffected; unrestrained; without art; as a natural manner.
Latin naturalis, from natura, from nascor, to be born — the root of nation, native, nature.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 2:14
But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
1 Corinthians 15:44
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.
James 1:23
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
Romans 1:26
For this cause God gave them up unto vile affections: for even their women did change the natural use into that which is against nature:
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 2:14 says the natural man cannot know the things of God, which is the exact point at which every synergistic account of conversion must soften the verb.
corruption_paragraphs: Neither can he know them. Paul does not say the natural man will not, or is unlikely to, but that he cannot, and he gives the reason: the things of the Spirit are spiritually discerned, and the natural man has no such faculty. This is total depravity stated as an epistemological fact, and it is why the Reformed tradition holds that regeneration precedes faith rather than following upon it. A man dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1) is not persuaded into life; he is raised. Every scheme that makes the decisive movement the sinner’s own — whether classical Arminianism with its universal enabling grace or the revivalist technique that treats conversion as a decision to be induced — must at this verse make cannot mean something less than it says. The free offer of the gospel is not thereby weakened; God ordinarily gives life through the preached word, which is exactly why it is preached to all.

Romans 1:26 uses natural in its other and now contested sense: the created order, from which a departure is against nature. Paul’s argument is not from custom or majority practice but from creation — God made them male and female (Genesis 1:27; Matthew 19:4), and marriage is one man and one woman for life. The affirming readings of this passage (Vines, Brownson and others) proceed by restricting Paul to exploitative or idolatrous forms of the practice, and the text will not narrow that way: the ground given is nature itself, and the same chapter has just described the exchange of the truth of God for a lie. This dictionary holds that line while distinguishing sharply between pastoral care for image-bearers caught in sin and doctrinal affirmation of the sin. Every person addressed in Romans 1 bears the image of God, and Romans 2 immediately forbids the reader to feel superior.
roots_summary: Greek psuchikos (G5591), belonging to the soul, natural, sensual; phusikos (G5446), according to nature; genesis (G1078), birth or origin; phusis (G5449), nature.
roots_lines: Greek psuchikos (G5591) — of the soul, natural as opposed to spiritual; the natural man (1 Corinthians 2:14) and a natural body (1 Corinthians 15:44).
Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual, of the Spirit; the deliberate contrast in both passages.
Greek phusikos (G5446) — according to nature; the natural use (Romans 1:26-27).
Greek phusis (G5449) — nature, the constitution of a thing as created (Romans 1:26).
Greek genesis (G1078) — birth, origin; his natural face, literally the face of his birth (James 1:23).
usage: The natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God... neither can he know them (1 Corinthians 2:14) — the impediment is capacity, not information.
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44) — not matter against spirit, but two animating principles.
Beholding his natural face in a glass (James 1:23) — the hearer who is not a doer, and forgets what he saw.

etymology: From Latin subjectus, thrown or placed under, from sub (under) and jacere (to throw). Webster 1828: placed or situate under; being under the power or dominion of another. The word states an order, and Scripture applies it to the creation, the citizen, and the incarnate Son.
biblical_def: Paul opens the thirteenth of Romans with a command addressed to every soul without exception: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God (Romans 13:1) — written to Christians in the imperial capital, under an emperor who would shortly kill many of them. The most remarkable use in Scripture, however, is of the Lord Himself. After the twelve-year-old Christ has astonished the doctors in the temple, Luke records: he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them (Luke 2:51). Eighteen years of the incarnate God submitting to a carpenter and his wife are summed in three words. Paul uses the word for the frustration laid on creation itself: the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope (Romans 8:20) — the subjection is God’s act and it is in hope, which is the whole difference between the biblical account of futility and a merely tragic one. Hebrews names the bondage Christ came to break: them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage (Hebrews 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUBJECT as placed or situate under; being under the power, control or dominion of another; hence liable, exposed, obedient; and as a verb, to bring under the power or dominion of.
webster_full: SUBJECT, a. — Placed or situate under.
Being under the power and dominion of another; as, Jamaica is subject to Great Britain.
Exposed; liable from extraneous causes; as, a country subject to extreme heat.
Obedient; submissive; as, be subject to the higher powers.
Latin subjectus, from sub, under, and jacio, to throw — the root of abject, project, reject.
scriptures: Romans 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Luke 2:51
And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
Romans 8:20
For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope,
Hebrews 2:15
And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.
corruption_summary: Romans 13:1 is abused in both directions — to demand unlimited obedience to any regime, and to be dismissed as a first-century accommodation — and the Reformed tradition has a careful answer to both.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 13 grounds civil authority in God’s ordination and commands subjection, and it does so without qualifying clauses about the ruler’s character — Nero was on the throne. But the same chapter defines the magistrate by his office: he is a minister of God for good, a revenger to execute wrath upon evildoers. Authority is delegated and bounded, and where a magistrate commands what God forbids, the apostles themselves answered that we ought to obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The Reformed doctrine of the lesser magistrate, worked out by Calvin, Knox, and the Vindiciae contra tyrannos, and by Samuel Rutherford in Lex Rex, provides for lawful resistance through subordinate authorities rather than private rebellion. What the tradition denies is the individual’s private right to nullify authority he dislikes, and equally the claim of any state to unconditioned obedience.

Luke 2:51 deserves more weight than it usually receives. The eternal Son, having just demonstrated in the temple that He knew His Father’s business, went home and was subject to Joseph and Mary for eighteen more years. Subjection here is not a mark of inferiority — the One subjected is God of God — which settles a question that recurs in every debate about order. The complementarian position this dictionary holds rests on exactly this: that headship and submission describe an ordering of equals, since the Son is subject to the Father and in no way less than the Father. Any account of submission that implies lesser worth has misread both the Trinity and Luke 2:51; and any account of equality that cannot tolerate order has misread them the other way.
roots_summary: Greek hupotasso (G5293), to arrange under, to subject; hupotage (G5292), subjection; enochos (G1777), held in, liable; Latin subjectus, placed under.
roots_lines: Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to arrange or set under, a military ordering term; be subject unto the higher powers (Romans 13:1) and was subject unto them (Luke 2:51).
Greek mataiotes (G3153) — vanity, futility, emptiness; what the creature was subjected to (Romans 8:20).
Greek elpis (G1680) — hope; the qualifier that distinguishes biblical futility from mere tragedy (Romans 8:20).
Greek enochos (G1777) — held in, liable to; subject to bondage (Hebrews 2:15).
Greek douleia (G1397) — bondage, slavery; the lifetime servitude broken by the resurrection (Hebrews 2:15).
usage: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers (Romans 13:1) — written to Christians under Nero.
He went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them (Luke 2:51) — eighteen years in three words.
The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly... in hope (Romans 8:20) — the subjection is God’s act, and it is in hope.

etymology: From Latin effectus, from efficere, to work out, to accomplish, from ex and facere, to do. Webster 1828: that which is produced by an agent or cause. The Authorized Version’s recurring phrase is of none effect — a thing rendered powerless without being formally denied.
biblical_def: Three times the New Testament warns that something may be made of none effect, and in each case the thing voided is precious. Our Lord names tradition as the agent: Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye (Mark 7:13). The scribes had not repealed the fifth commandment; they had built a rule about Corban that let a man evade it while appearing devout. Paul names law-keeping as the agent against promise: if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14) — inheritance by law and inheritance by promise cannot both stand, because they run on opposite principles. And he names his own eloquence as a possible agent against the cross: Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17). Against these Isaiah sets the positive: the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever (Isaiah 32:17).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EFFECT as that which is produced by an agent or cause; the event which follows immediately from an antecedent cause; consequence; result; also, purpose, general intent, or reality as opposed to appearance.
webster_full: EFFECT, n. — That which is produced by an agent or cause; the event which follows immediately from an antecedent cause.
Purpose; general intent; as, to this effect he spoke.
Consequence intended; utility; profit; advantage.
Reality; not mere appearance; as, in effect it is the same thing.
Latin effectus, from efficio, from ex and facio, to make — the root of efficient and efficacious.
scriptures: Mark 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
Romans 4:14
For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect:
1 Corinthians 1:17
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.
Isaiah 32:17
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.
corruption_summary: Mark 7:13 shows Scripture voided not by denial but by tradition laid alongside it, which is precisely the mechanism the Reformation identified in Rome and which no communion is immune to.
corruption_paragraphs: The scribes did not deny Honour thy father and thy mother; they added a rule that let a man declare his property Corban, a gift devoted to God, and so escape the duty while gaining a reputation for piety. The commandment stood on the page and was dead in practice. This is the essential Reformation argument against the elevation of tradition to a coordinate authority with Scripture: what is added does not merely supplement, it eventually overrules. Trent’s decree receiving unwritten traditions with equal affection and reverence as the written books is the formal version of the error our Lord names here. But no communion is safe from it. Wherever a confessional church allows a custom, a founder’s practice, or a house rule to become functionally unquestionable, the mechanism of Mark 7:13 is at work, and sola Scriptura is the standing remedy.

1 Corinthians 1:17 is the verse most often needed in the pulpit and least often applied. Paul feared that his own wisdom of words could empty the cross of its power — not contradict it, but void it, by shifting the hearer’s attention from the message to the performance. The modern equivalents are not eloquence alone but production, personality, and the sermon built to be memorable rather than to be true. The chapter’s argument is that God deliberately chose the foolishness of preaching and the offence of a crucified Messiah so that no flesh should glory in His presence. A ministry that succeeds by the very means Paul refused has not thereby proved him wrong; it has made the cross of none effect and called the result fruit.
roots_summary: Greek akuroo (G208), to make void, to deprive of authority; kenoo (G2758), to empty; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative; Hebrew abodah (H5656), work or service.
roots_lines: Greek akuroo (G208) — to deprive of force or authority, to make void; making the word of God of none effect (Mark 7:13).
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle or inoperative; the promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14).
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty out; lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17).
Greek korban (G2878) — a gift devoted to God; the device by which the commandment was evaded (Mark 7:11).
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — work, service, the thing wrought; the effect of righteousness (Isaiah 32:17).
usage: Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition (Mark 7:13) — the commandment left on the page and dead in practice.
The promise made of none effect (Romans 4:14) — law and promise run on opposite principles and cannot both be the ground.
Lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect (1 Corinthians 1:17) — Paul’s fear of his own eloquence.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon ceorfan, to cut, to hew. Webster 1828: cut into fanciful figures; engraved; sculptured. In Scripture the carved image is the second commandment’s standing offence, and the skill of the carver is never in doubt.
biblical_def: The carved image is the recurring object of Israel’s ruin, and Scripture never suggests it was crude. Micah’s house held a whole apparatus of devotion: these went into Micah's house, and fetched the carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image (Judges 18:18) — note that the ephod, a legitimate priestly garment, is in the same inventory as the idol, which is how syncretism always looks. Manasseh took the offence to its furthest point: he set a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God, of which God had said... In this house, and in Jerusalem... will I put my name for ever (2 Chronicles 33:7). The image is placed in the very house God had named for Himself. Moses commands the opposite treatment: ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire (Deuteronomy 7:5). The word also appears innocently, of ordinary furnishing, in the mouth of the strange woman: I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt (Proverbs 7:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CARVE as to cut into fanciful figures; to make by cutting, as an image; to engrave; hence CARVED, cut into shapes or figures; sculptured; engraved.
webster_full: CARVE, v.t. — To cut into fanciful figures; to make by cutting; as, to carve an image.
To engrave; to cut into a surface, as letters or figures.
To cut, as meat at table; to distribute in portions.
CARVED, pp. — Cut into images or figures; engraved; sculptured.
Anglo-Saxon ceorfan, to cut — related to carve, kerf, and Greek grapho, to cut or write.
scriptures: Judges 18:18
And these went into Micah's house, and fetched the carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image. Then said the priest unto them, What do ye?
2 Chronicles 33:7

And he set a carved image, the idol which he had made, in the house of God, of which God had said to David and to Solomon his son, In this house, and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen before all the tribes of Israel, will I put my name for ever:
Deuteronomy 7:5
But thus shall ye deal with them; ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images, and cut down their groves, and burn their graven images with fire.
Proverbs 7:16
I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt.
corruption_summary: The second commandment forbids images used in the worship of the true God, not only the worship of false gods, which is the point Rome’s distinction between veneration and adoration is designed to evade.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah’s house is the instructive case, because the man was not an atheist and not, in his own mind, an idolater. He had an ephod, a Levite for a priest, and a carved image, and Judges 17:13 records his conclusion: Now know I that the LORD will do me good, seeing I have a Levite to my priest. He was worshipping the LORD by means the LORD had not appointed. That is what the second commandment forbids, and it is distinct from the first: the first forbids other gods, the second forbids images in the worship of the true God. Rome’s answer — that images receive dulia or veneration rather than latria or adoration, and that the honour passes to the prototype — is a distinction the commandment does not make, and it is worth noting that the Roman catechetical tradition has commonly numbered the commandments so that this one disappears into the first.

Manasseh’s carved image in the temple is the extreme case, and Chronicles is careful to record God’s own words about that house before describing what was set in it. The narrative is also, remarkably, a story of grace: 2 Chronicles 33:12-13 says that in his affliction Manasseh besought the LORD, humbled himself greatly, and was heard and restored. The most flagrant idolater in Judah’s history repented and was received, which is why his account stands as one of Scripture’s strongest evidences that no sinner is beyond mercy. Reformation, when it came under Josiah, still had to remove what Manasseh had built — forgiveness of a man does not undo the consequences of his work in a nation.
roots_summary: Hebrew pesel (H6459), a carved or graven image; pasal (H6458), to hew or carve; massekah (H4541), a molten image; teraphim (H8655), household idols.
roots_lines: Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image; the object forbidden in the second commandment (Exodus 20:4).
Hebrew pasal (H6458) — to hew, to carve; the verb behind pesel, used also of hewing the second tables of stone.
Hebrew massekah (H4541) — a molten or cast image; the companion of the carved one in Micah’s house (Judges 18:18).
Hebrew teraphim (H8655) — household idols or images; part of the same inventory (Judges 18:18).
Hebrew asherah (H842) — a grove or wooden cult object; commanded to be cut down (Deuteronomy 7:5).
usage: The carved image, the ephod, and the teraphim, and the molten image (Judges 18:18) — the legitimate and the forbidden in one inventory.
He set a carved image... in the house of God (2 Chronicles 33:7) — in the very house God had named for Himself.
Burn their graven images with fire (Deuteronomy 7:5) — the appointed treatment, and it is not partial.

etymology: Past participle of tear, from Anglo-Saxon teran, to rend or pull apart. Webster 1828: pulled apart; rent; lacerated. In the law it is a technical term of the shepherd’s liability, and in Hosea it is what God does before He heals.
biblical_def: Hosea puts the hardest sentence about God’s dealings in the mouth of a repenting people, and does not soften it: Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up (Hosea 6:1). The tearing is acknowledged as God’s act; the returning is to the One who did it. There is no attempt to assign the wound elsewhere. In the law torn is a shepherd’s technical term. Jacob tells Laban he absorbed a loss the law would have excused: That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it (Genesis 31:39) — a hired shepherd could produce the carcase and be cleared, and Jacob paid instead. Flesh torn in the field was forbidden food: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs (Exodus 22:31). And Malachi records the final contempt of a priesthood offering what it would not have given a governor: ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the LORD (Malachi 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TEAR as to separate by violence or pulling; to rend; to lacerate; hence TORN, pulled apart, rent, lacerated, divided by violence.
webster_full: TEAR, v.t. — To separate by violence or by pulling; to rend; as, to tear cloth.
To lacerate; to wound; as, torn by briers.
To pull with violence; as, to tear the hair.
To divide by violent measures; to shatter; as, a state torn by factions.
TORN, pp. — Pulled apart; rent; lacerated. Anglo-Saxon teran, to tear.
scriptures: Hosea 6:1
Come, and let us return unto the LORD: for he hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up.
Genesis 31:39
That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it; of my hand didst thou require it, whether stolen by day, or stolen by night.
Exodus 22:31
And ye shall be holy men unto me: neither shall ye eat any flesh that is torn of beasts in the field; ye shall cast it to the dogs.
Malachi 1:13

Ye said also, Behold, what a weariness is it! and ye have snuffed at it, saith the LORD of hosts; and ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick; thus ye brought an offering: should I accept this of your hand? saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: Hosea 6:1 assigns the tearing to God and returns to Him for the healing, which no theology that must protect God from responsibility for affliction is able to say.
corruption_paragraphs: He hath torn, and he will heal us; he hath smitten, and he will bind us up. The repenting remnant does not say that the tearing came from circumstances, from enemies, or from a devil operating outside God’s permission; they name God as its author and go to Him for the cure. This is a sentence open theism cannot say, since it requires that the affliction was purposed; and it is a sentence the therapeutic frame cannot say, since it treats affliction as damage without design. The Reformed doctrine of providence permits it: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, including the affliction of His own people, without being the author of sin, and His purpose in wounding them is to bring them back. Job says the same in his own way, and Deuteronomy 32:39 states it flatly: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal.

Malachi 1:13 diagnoses a corruption of worship that is entirely compatible with continued attendance. The priests were still sacrificing; they were simply bringing what cost them nothing — the torn, the lame, the sick — and the LORD’s question is whether their governor would have accepted it (Malachi 1:8). The offence is not absence but contempt, and its outward form is indistinguishable from devotion. This is worth pressing because it is the likeliest form of the sin in a well-ordered church: attendance maintained, giving reduced to the remainder, attention given after everything else has taken its share. David’s refusal to offer what cost him nothing (2 Samuel 24:24) is the standing counterexample.
roots_summary: Hebrew taraph (H2963), to tear or rend, as a beast; terephah (H2966), that which is torn; gazal (H1497), to seize violently.
roots_lines: Hebrew taraph (H2963) — to tear in pieces, as a wild beast; he hath torn, and he will heal us (Hosea 6:1).
Hebrew terephah (H2966) — that which is torn, carrion; the technical term of the shepherd’s liability (Exodus 22:31).
Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to mend; the answering verb in Hosea 6:1.
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up, as a wound; the second answering verb in the same verse.
Hebrew pissach (H6455) — lame; joined to the torn and the sick in Malachi’s indictment (Malachi 1:13).
usage: He hath torn, and he will heal us (Hosea 6:1) — the tearing named as God’s act, and the return made to Him.
That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it (Genesis 31:39) — Jacob paying what the law would have excused.
Ye brought that which was torn, and the lame, and the sick (Malachi 1:13) — worship maintained and emptied of cost.

etymology: Plural of thief, from Anglo-Saxon theof. Webster 1828: those who take the property of another feloniously and secretly. Our Lord uses the word of the temple traders, of false shepherds, and of the fate of earthly treasure.
biblical_def: In the Sermon on the Mount thieves are the argument against a certain kind of investment: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal (Matthew 6:19). Three agents of loss are named — moth, rust and thieves — and the next verse locates the alternative where none of the three operate. Christ’s objection to earthly treasure is not that it is wicked to own but that it is foolish to trust, because the security is not real. He uses the word again in the cleansing of the temple, quoting Jeremiah: It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13) — the trade was legal, convenient, and conducted in the court where the Gentiles were meant to pray. In the shepherd discourse the term is applied to religious leaders: All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them (John 10:8), and the mark of the true sheep is that they did not follow. Paul lists thieves among those who shall not inherit the kingdom (1 Corinthians 6:10), and then says of the Corinthians, such were some of you.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines THIEF as one who secretly, unlawfully and feloniously takes the goods or personal property of another; distinguished from a robber, who takes by open force.
webster_full: THIEF, n. (pl. THIEVES) — One who secretly, unlawfully and feloniously takes the goods or personal property of another.
The thief takes by stealth; the robber takes by open force or violence.
One who seduces by false doctrine; a term applied in Scripture to false teachers.
THIEVISH, a. — Given to stealing; addicted to theft.
Anglo-Saxon theof; the same root as German Dieb.
scriptures: Matthew 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Matthew 21:13
And said unto them, It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
John 10:8
All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them.
1 Corinthians 6:10
Nor thieves, nor covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners, shall inherit the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 6:10 names sins that exclude from the kingdom and then says such were some of you, holding together a clarity and a mercy that the modern church usually manages only one of.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul lists thieves, the covetous, drunkards, revilers, extortioners and more, says plainly that such shall not inherit the kingdom of God, and then adds in the following verse: And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God (1 Corinthians 6:11). Both halves are required and each is commonly lost without the other. Where the list is softened — treated as culturally bound, or as describing patterns rather than persons — the warning disappears and with it the urgency of the gospel. Where the list is preached without verse 11, the church becomes a place no former thief believes he may enter. The apostolic pattern is to name the sin exactly, deny that its practitioners inherit, and then declare that some of the congregation used to be exactly that and are washed.

Matthew 21:13 deserves attention for what the traders were actually doing. Selling approved animals and exchanging foreign coin for temple currency was lawful, useful, and answered a genuine need of pilgrims. The offence lay in where it was done — the court of the Gentiles, the one place in the temple where the nations could pray — and in what it had become, a concession turned into a market. Christ’s quotation joins Isaiah 56:7, which calls the house a house of prayer for all people, to Jeremiah 7:11. The application to a church is not far to seek: the useful thing set up in the space appointed for prayer, and defended because it meets a need, is the exact configuration our Lord overturned.
roots_summary: Greek kleptes (G2812), a thief who takes by stealth; lestes (G3027), a robber or brigand who takes by force; Hebrew gannab (H1590), a thief; parits (H6530), a violent one.
roots_lines: Greek kleptes (G2812) — one who steals by stealth; thieves break through and steal (Matthew 6:19), the root of English kleptomania.
Greek lestes (G3027) — a robber or brigand, taking by open violence; a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13) uses this word.
Hebrew gannab (H1590) — a thief; the subject of the eighth commandment’s prohibition.
Hebrew parits (H6530) — a violent or ravenous one; a den of robbers in Jeremiah 7:11, the verse Christ quotes.
Greek diorusso (G1358) — to dig through, as through a mud wall; the vivid verb behind break through (Matthew 6:19).
usage: Where thieves break through and steal (Matthew 6:19) — the objection to earthly treasure is that the security is not real.
Ye have made it a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13) — a lawful trade set up in the court appointed for the nations to pray.
All that ever came before me are thieves and robbers: but the sheep did not hear them (John 10:8) — the mark of the sheep is that they did not follow.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon laenan, to grant for a time, from laen, a loan. Webster 1828: to grant to another for temporary use, on the express or implied condition that the thing shall be returned. The law of Israel bent the ordinary terms of lending toward the poor, and Christ removed them altogether.
biblical_def: The Mosaic law treats lending to a poor Israelite as an obligation rather than an opportunity: thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth (Deuteronomy 15:8) — and the surrounding verses forbid the calculation that the year of release is near. Interest is excluded outright in such a case: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury (Exodus 22:25). The Psalter makes lending a mark of the righteous man rather than a risk he takes: He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed (Psalm 37:26). Our Lord then removes the last remaining expectation: love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil (Luke 6:35). The ground given is not the borrower’s worthiness but the Father’s character, and the imitation is the point.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEND as to grant to another for temporary use, on the express or implied condition that the thing shall be returned; to afford or grant; to permit to use for a time.
webster_full: LEND, v.t. — To grant to another for temporary use, on the condition that the thing shall be returned; as, to lend a book.
To grant money for temporary use, usually on interest.
To afford; to grant; to furnish; as, to lend assistance.
To let for hire or compensation; as, to lend a horse.
Anglo-Saxon laenan, from laen, a loan — the root of English loan.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 15:8
But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth.
Exodus 22:25
If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.
Psalm 37:26
He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed.
Luke 6:35

But love ye your enemies, and do good, and lend, hoping for nothing again; and your reward shall be great, and ye shall be the children of the Highest: for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil.
corruption_summary: Luke 6:35 commands lending without expectation of return, and its ground is the Father’s kindness to the unthankful — which is precisely the argument the merit-based instinct in charity refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: Lend, hoping for nothing again. The command is given in the same breath as loving enemies and doing good, and the reason attached is that God is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil. Christian giving is therefore modelled on a kindness that its recipients have not earned and will not repay, which cuts against the instinct — strong and often dressed as prudence — to make help conditional on the recipient’s deserving. Scripture is not naive about this: it commands work (2 Thessalonians 3:10), warns against sloth throughout Proverbs, and expects wisdom in the exercise of mercy. But the wisdom governs the method, not the disposition, and a church whose giving is limited to the demonstrably deserving has adopted a standard by which it would itself have received nothing.

The Old Testament’s prohibition of usury to a poor brother has been the subject of long debate, and the Reformed tradition’s handling of it is worth stating. Calvin, examining Exodus 22:25 and its parallels, concluded that Scripture forbids the oppressive lending that exploits a brother’s need, not every charge for the productive use of capital, and the distinction has largely held in Protestant economic thought. What cannot be evaded is the text’s protective intent: the poor man is not a market. Deuteronomy 15:9 goes further and warns against the thought that rises in a wicked heart — that the year of release is at hand, and so the brother may be given nought. The calculation about repayment was accurate; the heart that let it govern a decision about need is what Scripture names.
roots_summary: Hebrew lavah (H3867), to join, to borrow or lend; nashak (H5391), to bite, and so to lend on interest; Greek daneizo (G1155), to lend on interest; kichremi (G5531), to lend as a friendly act.
roots_lines: Hebrew lavah (H3867) — to join oneself to, and so to borrow or lend; the standing verb of Deuteronomy 15:8.
Hebrew nashak (H5391) — to bite; the same root gives neshek, interest, which bites the borrower (Exodus 22:25).
Hebrew chanan (H2603) — to show favour, to be gracious; the merciful lending of Psalm 37:26.
Greek daneizo (G1155) — to lend, ordinarily at interest; the verb Christ redefines in Luke 6:35.
Greek apelpizo (G560) — to give up hope of, to expect nothing back; hoping for nothing again (Luke 6:35).
usage: Thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him (Deuteronomy 15:8) — lending to the poor as obligation, not opportunity.
Thou shalt not be to him as an usurer (Exodus 22:25) — the poor man is not a market.
Lend, hoping for nothing again... for he is kind unto the unthankful and to the evil (Luke 6:35) — the ground is the Father’s character.

etymology: From Middle English on his halve, on his side or part, from Anglo-Saxon healf, side, half. Webster 1828: favor; benefit; advantage; also, part, side, in the phrase in behalf of. Paul uses it for the thing given to believers on Christ’s account, and the gift is a surprising one.
biblical_def: Philippians contains one of the most bracing sentences in the New Testament, and it turns on this word: For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake (Philippians 1:29). Two things are given — the verb is one of grace, the same root as the word for gift — and the second of them is suffering. Believing and suffering arrive together on Christ’s account, and Paul presents the second as a grant rather than a misfortune. Peter draws the practical consequence for a Christian under accusation: if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf (1 Peter 4:16) — the very name then used as a slander becomes the ground of glorifying God. Paul also uses the word for ordinary gladness over a church: your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf (Romans 16:19), and for the credit he wanted the Corinthians to be able to give: we... give you occasion to glory on our behalf (2 Corinthians 5:12).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BEHALF as favor; benefit; advantage; and in the phrase in behalf of, in the name of, on the part of, for the sake or interest of another.
webster_full: BEHALF, n. — Favor; benefit; advantage; as, he pleaded in his behalf.
Part; side; used with in or on; as, in behalf of the poor.
In the name of; on the part of; as, to act on behalf of another.
The word implies representation — one standing in the place or interest of another.
Middle English on his halve, from Anglo-Saxon healf, side.
scriptures: Philippians 1:29
For unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ, not only to believe on him, but also to suffer for his sake;
1 Peter 4:16
Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.
Romans 16:19
For your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf: but yet I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil.
2 Corinthians 5:12
For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart.
corruption_summary: Philippians 1:29 calls suffering for Christ a thing given, in the vocabulary of grace, which no theology that treats affliction as an anomaly to be removed can accommodate.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek verb is charizomai, from charis, grace — the word for a favour freely bestowed. Paul says two things have been graciously granted to the Philippians on Christ’s account: believing, and suffering. That the second stands in the same clause as the first, governed by the same verb, is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the apostolic estimate of persecution. Prosperity teaching cannot say this sentence and neither can the softer assumption, common in comfortable churches, that suffering for the faith represents a failure of strategy or of favour. Nor is Paul writing theoretically: he is in prison as he writes, and tells the same church a chapter later that he counts all things loss. The 1689 Confession’s chapter on providence anticipates exactly this, speaking of God ordering affliction to His children for holy ends.

1 Peter 4:16 records a small and important detail: Christian is used here as the accusers’ word. It occurs only three times in the New Testament, twice on the lips of outsiders (Acts 11:26; Acts 26:28) and here in the context of legal accusation. Peter’s instruction is to take the slander and glorify God on that very account — not to dispute the label but to wear it. The pattern recurs whenever a name applied in contempt is received and redeemed, and it is worth remembering when believers grow anxious about how they are described. The apostolic response to being badly named is neither indignation nor rebranding; it is to suffer under the name without shame and to glorify God on this behalf.
roots_summary: Greek huper (G5228), on behalf of, for the sake of; charizomai (G5483), to grant as a favour; meros (G3313), a part or portion; onoma (G3686), a name.
roots_lines: Greek huper (G5228) — on behalf of, in the interest of; the preposition rendered in the behalf of Christ (Philippians 1:29).
Greek charizomai (G5483) — to grant freely as a favour, from charis, grace; the verb governing both believing and suffering.
Greek meros (G3313) — a part, a portion, a respect; on this behalf (1 Peter 4:16).
Greek Christianos (G5546) — Christian; used only three times, twice by outsiders (Acts 11:26; Acts 26:28).
Greek aischuno (G153) — to be ashamed; what the sufferer is forbidden to be (1 Peter 4:16).
usage: Unto you it is given in the behalf of Christ... also to suffer for his sake (Philippians 1:29) — suffering granted in the vocabulary of grace.
Let him glorify God on this behalf (1 Peter 4:16) — the slander received and turned to praise.
I am glad therefore on your behalf (Romans 16:19) — and the same verse asks for wisdom about good and simplicity about evil.

etymology: From here and by: by this; by means of this. Webster 1828: by this. John uses it as the recurring signal of his epistle, introducing the tests by which a believer may know where he stands.
biblical_def: First John is written that its readers may know (1 John 5:13), and hereby is the word that introduces the evidence. It defines love by pointing at the cross: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren (1 John 3:16) — and the second clause follows from the first without a pause, because the definition carries an obligation. It supplies the doctrinal test for spirits: Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God (1 John 4:2). The test is Christological and it is objective; no impression, power or manifestation substitutes for the confession. It supplies the test of obedience: whoso keepeth his word, in him verily is the love of God perfected: hereby know we that we are in him (1 John 2:5). And it addresses the anxious conscience directly: hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him (1 John 3:19), the following verses adding that if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEREBY as by this; by means of this; by this thing or means — introducing the ground on which something is known or effected.
webster_full: HEREBY, adv. — By this.
By means of this; by this thing, fact or circumstance.
Compare THEREBY, by that; WHEREBY, by which.
In legal usage it marks the instrument by which a thing is effected.
From here and by.
scriptures: 1 John 3:16
Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.
1 John 4:2
Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God:
1 John 2:5
But whoso keepeth his word, in him verily is the love of God perfected: hereby know we that we are in him.
1 John 3:19
And hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him.
corruption_summary: 1 John supplies objective tests of assurance — doctrine, obedience, and love of the brethren — against both the mysticism that tests by experience and the mere professionalism that tests by nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: John gives three recurring marks, and they work together: right confession about Christ come in the flesh, keeping His commandments, and love of the brethren. Each is objective enough to be examined. This is the Reformed doctrine of assurance in apostolic form — resting on the promises of God, evidenced by the inward graces, sealed by the Spirit — and it stands against two failures. The first is the mystical test, which locates certainty in the intensity of an experience; 1 John 4:1 explicitly forbids believing every spirit and gives a doctrinal criterion instead. The second is the assurance that rests on a past transaction alone, with no present evidence sought or expected; John writes his letter precisely so that believers may know, and he does not tell them to look back at a decision. The 1689 Confession follows him closely, warning that a man may deceive himself with false hopes while promising that infallible assurance is attainable.

1 John 3:19-20 is the pastoral heart of the matter and is frequently misquoted. John says that hereby we know we are of the truth and shall assure our hearts before him, and then adds: For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. The comfort is not that the accusing heart is mistaken about the sin — it may be quite right — but that God’s knowledge is larger than the heart’s and includes the work of His own grace in a believer that the believer cannot presently see. This is the answer to a tender conscience, and it is a different answer from the one the therapeutic instinct supplies, which would relieve the condemnation by lowering the standard. John relieves it by appealing over the heart’s head to God.
roots_summary: Greek en touto, in this, by this; ginosko (G1097), to know by experience; homologeo (G3670), to confess or say the same thing; peitho (G3982), to persuade or assure.
roots_lines: Greek en touto — in this, by this; the phrase rendered hereby throughout 1 John.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, often by acquaintance or evidence; the recurring verb of John’s tests.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to say the same thing, to confess; the doctrinal criterion of 1 John 4:2.
Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade, and so to assure; shall assure our hearts before him (1 John 3:19).
Greek kataginosko (G2607) — to condemn, to find fault against; the accusing heart of 1 John 3:20.
usage: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us (1 John 3:16) — the definition carries its obligation in the next clause.
Hereby know ye the Spirit of God (1 John 4:2) — the test is Christological and objective.
Hereby we know that we are of the truth, and shall assure our hearts before him (1 John 3:19) — addressed to the anxious conscience.
